title: The Sage With Eyes in His Feet
hookLine: a thinker walks into a well, and a school of logic begins by asking how we know
carry: nyaya: four ways of knowing, aimed at freedom
tomorrow: how did Yudhishthira know the house would burn?

cards: There's a playful old legend about Gautama, the sage tradition credits with the Nyaya Sutra. He was so lost in thought, the story goes, that he walked straight into a well. He climbed out and went right back to thinking.
So, the legend says, he was given eyes in his feet, to think and walk at the same time. That's why he's also called Akshapada, eye-footed. It's a joke about philosophers, told with love.
And under it sits a real question: when you say you know something, where did that knowing come from?

teach.b: This part of the path is the six darshanas. Darshana means seeing, and here a way of seeing: a school of Hindu thought. We'll take them one at a time, side by side, and rank none of them.
Nyaya, the school of logic, comes first only because we have to start somewhere.
The Nyaya Sutra opens with a list of what it will examine, and the very first is pramana: a means of knowing, a way real knowledge reaches you. It names four.
Perception: what you see, hear and touch yourself, like the well in front of your feet. Inference: reasoning from a sign to what you can't see, smoke on a hill, so fire behind it.
Comparison: knowing a new thing by its likeness to one you know; the commentators' example is a traveler told that a certain forest animal looks like a cow, who recognizes it when he meets one.
And word: the testimony of someone reliable. For Nyaya, that includes the Veda. Here's what surprises people.
Scripture isn't set against reason here; it's one of reason's four doors, and the four check each other. And near its start, this book of logic says its aim is release, freedom from suffering.
False knowledge leads to faults, faults to action, action to birth, birth to suffering. Remove the false knowledge at the bottom and the whole chain comes loose.
So when someone says Hindus just believe things on faith, here's a Hindu school that asked first: how do I know this, and through which door did it come in?

how: In traditional Sanskrit learning, students study Nyaya through the Nyaya Sutra and its commentaries, beginning with the means of knowing and learning to test an argument with a teacher.

o: a school of logic that asks how we know, aiming at release
a school of logic that sees reasoning as a block to release
a school of debate whose goal is winning every argument

games.q: Nyaya's four means of knowing — tap the pairs.
p: inference: from a sign to the unseen
comparison: like a cow, so that's it
word: reliable testimony, including the Veda

s: Nyaya's goal is simply winning debates
the Nyaya Sutra says its aim is release, freedom from suffering, by removing false knowledge.
the Nyaya Sutra names four means of knowing
for Nyaya, scripture and reasoning are enemies
word, including the Veda, is one of its four means of knowing, alongside seeing and inference.

games.q: a traveler is told a certain forest animal looks like a cow. deep in the forest, he meets one and knows what it is. which means of knowing did he use?
games.why: upamana, comparison: knowing a new thing by its likeness to one already known. it's the commentators' example.

practice: Bring to mind something you're sure of today, about a person, about tomorrow, about yourself, and ask quietly where it came from: did you see it, reason to it from a sign, match it to something you knew, or were you told, and by someone how reliable?
Don't argue with it; just find its source, and notice whether its sources agree. If you pray, you can ask the God you know for clear sight.

wordCard.voice: Nyaya. The school of logic, which begins by asking how we know, names four means of knowing, and says the goal of clear thinking is freedom from suffering.

orig.note: Sanskrit: pramana, a means of valid knowing; Nyaya's first topic.

carryVoice: Your line: Nyaya, four ways of knowing, aimed at freedom. Clear thinking can be a path, too. Rest well.
